687.title: What you keep
687.hook: three Stoic habits that fit your life
687.howItsDone: Some people finishing a period of Stoic study choose a small number of practices, often three, that they will keep using daily, and write them down.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where the Stoics stop, the honest edge of the map. Your line was what it leaves open. Did you write your open question down? Day six hundred eighty-seven.

Open almost any kitchen drawer and you'll find the gadgets: a garlic press, an egg slicer, a cherry pitter used once. Then there's what actually gets reached for every night: one good knife, one pan, a wooden spoon. Nobody plans that short list. Use writes it. This year on the path has handed you a lot: morning previews, evening questions, two handles, two cities, the view from above, the ripe olive. Most of it can stay in the drawer. Today: what you keep.
screen: `A DRAWER FULL OF GADGETS.` → `ONE KNIFE, ONE PAN, ONE SPOON.` → `A YEAR OF PRACTICES.`

segments.voice: First, Seneca's advice on books. In one of his earliest letters to Lucilius, he warns against reading too many authors, skipping from one to the next. Food that's thrown up as soon as it's swallowed, he says, doesn't nourish. A plant moved too often never grows. Better to stay with a few great minds and digest them. And each day, choose one thought to carry. That's the spirit of this week: not everything, but a few things, really digested. Second, Epictetus on training. The Stoic word is askēsis: practice, training, the way an athlete trains. Every habit, Epictetus says, is built up and strengthened by the matching actions: walking by walking, running by running. If you want to be good at something, do it. If you don't want a habit, stop feeding it. So the habits you keep are the ones you'll actually do, not the ones you admire. Third, how to choose your three. Ask three questions of each practice from the year. Did I actually use it? Did it change a real day, even once? Does it fit the life I have, with my work, my family, my body, my beliefs? Someone might keep the evening review, the two columns, and delaying an angry reply. Someone else, the morning preview, the view from above, and love for the mortal. There's no right three. Fourth, why three. Few enough to remember without a list. Enough to cover morning, evening and the hard moments in between. Epictetus told his students not to talk about their principles, but to show them by how they live. Three is a number you can show.
screen: `DIGEST A FEW, DON'T SAMPLE MANY.` · `ASKĒSIS: HABITS BUILT BY DOING.` · `USED IT? CHANGED A DAY? FITS MY LIFE?` · `THREE YOU CAN SHOW, NOT TELL.` · then, large: `MY THREE.`

segments.voice: Let the year's practices pass slowly through your mind, like utensils laid out on a counter. The morning preview. The evening questions. The two columns. The other handle. The view from above. Delay. Both cities. Begin now. Notice which ones your hand actually reached for on hard days. Pick up three, one at a time, and keep them out on the counter. Put the others back in the drawer; you're not throwing them away. The bell holds the time.
What you keep: the three Stoic habits from this year that actually fit your life, chosen to be practiced, not admired. Today's word.
Your line: my three. Write your three habits down today, on paper or your phone, somewhere you'll see them next week. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

688.title: What you leave
688.hook: one Stoic idea that doesn't fit you
688.howItsDone: Some modern readers of the Stoics adopt some of their practices while openly setting aside others, such as the ideal of being free of all passions or the paradox that all wrongs are equal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what you keep, three habits out on the counter. Your line was my three. Did you write them down somewhere you'll see them? Day six hundred eighty-eight.

A friend lends you a cookbook from their grandmother's kitchen. You love it. You make the bread every Sunday now. But there's a chapter on organ meats that you read once, out of respect, and quietly decided was not for you. You didn't throw the book away. You didn't write an angry letter to the grandmother. You just left that chapter where it was. A year of Stoic reading can leave a chapter like that: an idea admired, or tried, or argued with, and finally set down. Today: what you leave.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER'S COOKBOOK.` → `BREAD EVERY SUNDAY.` → `ONE CHAPTER, LEFT WHERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: First, permission from Seneca himself. He was a committed Stoic, and still he wrote that he hadn't bound himself to any one master or borne anyone's name. In another letter he says the great thinkers who came before us are not our masters but our guides. And he quoted Epicurus, a rival, again and again, taking what was good wherever he found it. Leaving something behind is, oddly, a very Senecan thing to do. Second, some candidates. Some readers find a few Stoic ideas hard to live with. The hope of being entirely free of passions, which can sound like numbness. The claim that health, wealth, even the people we love, are indifferent to our true good. The old Stoic paradox that all wrongdoing is equally wrong. Epictetus's hardest words about grief. None of these is a misreading; they really are in the texts. And serious Stoics, then and now, have argued about them too. Third, how to leave well. Not with contempt. Name the idea fairly, in its strongest form, the way the Stoics would have stated it. Then say plainly, without a fight: not for me. You may come back to it in ten years and find it fits. Or not. Fourth, why this matters. Seneca read his teachers this way, as guides, keeping some things and leaving others, and the Stoic school itself kept arguing with its founders. Walking a philosophy as yourself is part of the tradition, not a break from it. The porch was always open on the sides. You can step off it, and step back on.
screen: `NOT OUR MASTERS, BUT OUR GUIDES.` · `SOME IDEAS ARE HARD TO LIVE WITH.` · `NAME IT FAIRLY, THEN SET IT DOWN.` · `WALK THE PATH AS YOURSELF.` · then, large: `NOT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Think back over the year for one Stoic idea that never sat right with you. Let it come into view. Now state it, silently, in its strongest and fairest form, the way a good Stoic would. Notice that you can understand it and still not take it on. Then, gently, set it down, the way you'd close a chapter in a borrowed book. Say to yourself: not for me, at least not now. Notice what that leaves. The bell holds the time.
What you leave: one Stoic idea, named fairly and set down without contempt, because the old teachers are guides, not masters. Today's word.

689.title: A year on the porch
689.hook: a year with Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus
689.howItsDone: Some people finishing a year of Stoic reading reread their earliest notes and ask how the practice has changed them, if at all.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what you leave, one idea set down fairly. Your line was not for me. Did you write it beside your three, with one kind sentence? Day six hundred eighty-nine.

A merchant from Cyprus named Zeno has been shipwrecked and lost his cargo. Stranded in Athens, he wanders into a bookshop and hears someone reading about Socrates. He asks the bookseller: where can I find men like that? The story goes that a philosopher happened to walk past right then, and the bookseller pointed. Years later, Zeno began teaching in a public colonnade on the edge of the marketplace. That covered walkway gave the school its name, and gave this whole year its name too. Today: a year on the porch.
screen: `A SHIPWRECKED MERCHANT.` → `WHERE CAN I FIND MEN LIKE THAT?` → `A COLONNADE IN ATHENS.`

segments.voice: First, the porch itself. In Greek, stoa poikilē: the painted porch, a long roofed walkway whose walls carried famous paintings, including the battle of Marathon. Anyone could walk in. Zeno taught there, in public, and his followers were called the people of the stoa: Stoics. A philosophy named not after a founder but after a public place where anyone could stand and listen. Second, the road we walked. We started on day three hundred thirty-two with a little handbook, Epictetus's teaching boiled down by his student Arrian, meant to be kept at hand. Then the longer Discourses, Epictetus arguing and joking with his students. Then Seneca, letter by letter, essay by essay. Then all twelve books of Marcus, straight through. And lately, the wider porch: the founders before, the neighbors next door, the people who came after, the turning year, and the porch in ordinary life. Third, four very different voices. A merchant who lost everything at sea. A man once enslaved, who limped. A rich adviser at a dangerous court. An emperor writing to himself on campaign. They didn't agree on everything, and they weren't saints. But each of them kept asking the same plain questions: what is up to me? What is good? How should I live with other people? Fourth, what a year does. One lesson is a thought. A year of them is a road, with your own days woven through it. Before we thank each teacher by name, it's worth looking back at where you started, and seeing how far the porch has run.
screen: `STOA POIKILĒ: THE PAINTED PORCH.` · `HANDBOOK, DISCOURSES, LETTERS, NOTEBOOK.` · `FOUR VOICES, THE SAME PLAIN QUESTIONS.` · `A YEAR OF DAYS, WOVEN IN.` · then, large: `A YEAR ON THE PORCH.`

segments.voice: Go back, in your mind or in your notes, to day three hundred thirty-two, the handbook for the road. Its line was keep it at hand. What were you carrying then? What was hard in your life? Now look at today. What's changed, even slightly? Maybe nothing obvious; that's honest too. Then let the year's voices pass by, Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca, Marcus, and notice which one, if any, you'd most like to sit beside. The bell holds the time.
A year on the porch: a year in the school named for Athens' painted porch, with Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus, walked one day at a time. Today's word.

690.title: Thank the freed slave
690.hook: Epictetus, lame and once enslaved, taught an emperor through a book
690.howItsDone: Some readers of Epictetus keep in mind that he was once enslaved and never wrote anything himself, and use that as a prompt to thank the unlikely people who have taught them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a year on the porch, back to the handbook where we started. Your line was a year on the porch. What did your first page say? Day six hundred ninety.

Emperors had famous teachers: senators, celebrated scholars with big houses. This one's favorite reading came from somewhere else. A slave in Nero's Rome, walking with a limp. He never writes a book. He's eventually freed, teaches in Rome, is driven out of the city along with the other philosophers, and opens a school in a provincial town in Greece. And an emperor of Rome ends up reading his words, and thanks the friend who shared them. Today begins three days of thanks. Today: thank the freed slave.
screen: `A SLAVE IN NERO'S ROME, WITH A LIMP.` → `FREED, EXILED, TEACHING IN GREECE.` → `AN EMPEROR READING HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, his name. Epiktētos is an ordinary Greek word meaning acquired, and some readers hear in it a slave's name: something bought. We don't know what his parents called him. Tradition says his owner was Epaphroditus, a freedman who served Nero. In the Discourses, Epictetus remembers his teacher Musonius Rufus testing him with the question: what will you do when your master treats you badly? Second, his limp. Ancient writers didn't agree on how it happened. One story, preserved by Origen, says a master twisted his leg until it broke, while Epictetus calmly warned him it would. Another says it was illness. Nobody knows for sure. What we do know is that the man who taught that lameness hinders the leg, not the will, was speaking from his own body. Third, the book he didn't write. Epictetus wrote nothing. His student Arrian took down his words as closely as he could, as reminders for himself. In the letter at the front of the Discourses, Arrian says the notes reached the public without his knowledge. Those notes, and the little Handbook we opened this year with, are nearly all we have of Epictetus. Fourth, the emperor. In the first book of the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius thanks his teacher Rusticus for many things, among them for introducing him to Epictetus's teaching, sharing it from his own copy. So the chain goes: an enslaved man, a teacher, a student's notes, a friend's copy, an emperor's notebook, and, centuries later, you. The person at the start of that chain is the one nobody would have bet on. That's worth a moment of thanks. And it's worth wondering who the unlikely teachers in your own life have been.
screen: `EPIKTĒTOS: ACQUIRED.` · `THE LIMP: SOURCES DIFFER.` · `ARRIAN'S NOTES, NOT HIS BOOK.` · `RUSTICUS SHARED EPICTETUS WITH MARCUS.` · then, large: `THE UNLIKELY TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who taught you something important, but who you never would have expected to. A grandparent with little schooling. A coworker everyone overlooked. A child. A stranger on a bus. Someone you once looked down on. Picture them clearly. What did they teach you, in words or just by how they lived? If thanks comes, let it go toward them. If they're still living, think how you might tell them. The bell holds the time.

691.title: Thank the courtier
691.hook: Seneca, flawed and rich, left the kindest letters
691.howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca hold both his wisdom and his compromises in view at once, valuing the letters while seeing the man clearly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: thank the freed slave, Epictetus, the most unlikely link in the chain. Your line was the unlikely teacher. Whom did you thank? Day six hundred ninety-one.

A coach who changed your life and also yelled too much. A professor whose ideas you still use, and who turned out to have behaved badly. A parent who taught kindness and wasn't always kind. Teachers like that are hard to put on a pedestal, and hard to throw away. Some readers put Seneca in exactly that spot. He wrote letters full of warmth and good sense. He was also enormously rich, and he spent years at the side of Nero. Today: thank the courtier.
screen: `A COACH WHO YELLED TOO MUCH.` → `NOT A PEDESTAL, NOT THE TRASH.` → `SENECA AT NERO'S SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the flaws, said plainly. Seneca was enormously wealthy, and ancient critics accused him of hypocrisy for preaching simplicity from his villas. He was Nero's tutor and then his adviser, and stayed on through dark years; the historian Tacitus reports that after Nero had his own mother killed, Seneca was believed to have written the letter Nero sent the Senate explaining it away. Earlier, exiled to Corsica, he wrote a consolation to a powerful official that reads, in places, like flattery aimed at winning his way home. Second, he knew. Seneca imagines his critics asking why he talks one way and lives another. He answers that he isn't wise, and isn't even close. He speaks about virtue, he says, not about himself, and when he criticizes faults, he includes his own. Third, the kindness. The letters to Lucilius are full of it: the people who serve us are human beings like us; tears for a friend are allowed; begin now; trust a true friend as you trust yourself. Fourth, the end. Later, accused of a part in a plot against Nero, Seneca was ordered to die. Tacitus tells us he asked for tablets to write his will and was refused. So he turned to his friends and said that since he couldn't repay them, he would leave them the one thing he still had, and the finest: the pattern of his life. Flawed and kind. Both true. You can hold them together, thank him for the letters, and still see the man clearly.
screen: `RICH, AND AT NERO'S SIDE.` · `I'M NOT WISE, NOT EVEN CLOSE.` · `THE KINDEST LETTERS.` · `THE PATTERN OF HIS LIFE.` · then, large: `FLAWED AND KIND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one flawed teacher in your own life: a parent, a coach, a boss, a mentor. Let both sides come into view. What they gave you. Where they fell short, or did harm. Don't erase either side. Then, if you're ready, let a small forgiveness loosen something, not saying it was fine, just letting go of a little of the weight. If you're not ready, simply hold both sides, honestly. That's enough today. The bell holds the time.
Thank the courtier: thanks to Seneca, rich and compromised at Nero's court, who still left letters full of kindness. Today's word.

692.title: Thank the emperor
692.hook: Marcus wrote to no one and ended up writing to everyone
692.howItsDone: Many readers of the Meditations keep a private notebook of their own, writing short lines to themselves in the second person, the way Marcus did.

segments.voice: Yesterday: thank the courtier, Seneca, rich and flawed and kind. Your line was flawed and kind. Did you let one imperfect teacher off the hook, even a little? Day six hundred ninety-two.

A tent on the Danube frontier, sometime in the 170s, after dark. The man inside is the emperor of Rome, and he is writing in a private notebook, in Greek, to nobody. Not to the Senate. Not to his son. To himself. Get up, there's work to do. You'll meet difficult people today. You're getting angry again. Nobody was meant to read it. Today it sits on nightstands and in backpacks around the world. The third and last of our thank-yous: thank the emperor.
screen: `A TENT ON THE FRONTIER, AFTER DARK.` → `WRITING TO NOBODY.` → `READ AROUND THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: First, a notebook with no reader. Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from 161 to 180, and spent much of his last decade at war in the north. Two of the books carry small notes of where they were written: among the Quadi, by the river Granua, and at Carnuntum, an army base on the Danube. He never mentions publishing. He talks to himself as you, the way you talk to yourself in the car. Second, how close it came to vanishing. After his death the notebook goes almost silent in the record for centuries. Around the year 900, a Byzantine bishop named Arethas writes in a letter that he owns an old copy, worn and battered. As we saw back on day 521, the first printed edition came out in 1559 from a manuscript that is now lost. A private book, hanging by a thread. Third, why it reaches everyone. Because he wasn't performing. A speech has to look good. A note to yourself only has to be true. So Marcus admits things. Again and again he tells himself to stop getting angry. In book eight he orders himself: let no one hear you complaining about life at court any more, not even you. The ruler of an empire, caught grumbling, and catching himself. That honesty is what travels across eighteen centuries to someone reading on a bus. Fourth, how to thank him. Book one is itself a page of thanks: to his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, his adoptive father, and the gods, each for something specific. So the fitting thanks is his own kind. Name one specific thing he gave you. For many readers it's this: you can talk to yourself firmly and kindly, in plain words, and get up again.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK WITH NO READER.` · `ARETHAS AND A WORN OLD COPY.` · `NOT PERFORMING, SO IT TRAVELS.` · `THANK HIM HIS OWN WAY.` · then, large: `TO HIMSELF, TO US.`

segments.voice: Find something to write on: a note on your phone, the back of a receipt. Think of one thing you've needed to hear lately. Not a slogan. Something specific, the way Marcus wrote: you're tired, so rest before you answer. You said you'd call your brother. Write one line to yourself, as you, plain and kind. Read it once, slowly. Then put the pen down and sit with it. You don't have to show anyone. He didn't. The bell holds the time.

693.title: Where it worked
693.hook: where did Stoic practice actually change a day?
693.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a journal and note specific moments when a principle changed what they did, as evidence of progress rather than knowledge.

segments.voice: Yesterday: thank the emperor, the notebook Marcus wrote to nobody. Your line was to himself, to us. Did you read your own line again before bed? Day six hundred ninety-three. The end of the week.

What would count as evidence? A runner can show a race time. A baker can show the bread. A year of Stoic reading has no scoreboard. Its evidence is quieter: a sharp remark someone didn't make, a night someone slept instead of rehearsing an argument, a loss met a little more steadily. Nobody hands out medals for those, and they're easy to forget by the weekend. So today we go looking for them on purpose, one at a time. Where did it actually work?
screen: `NO SCOREBOARD FOR THIS.` → `A SHARP REMARK, NOT MADE.` → `WHERE DID IT ACTUALLY WORK?`

segments.voice: First, the Stoics' own test. Epictetus was blunt about where progress shows. Not in how many books you've read, he says in the Discourses, but in what you do with your desires and fears, in how you meet the day. In the Handbook he gives the picture we met back on day 381: sheep don't bring their grass back up to show the shepherd how much they ate. They digest it, and give wool and milk. So the question isn't what you know about Stoicism. It's where the wool showed. Second, the evidence is small. Look back down the year at the tools: a reply delayed, from Stoic in anger. A worry sorted into two columns, from Stoic at work. The evening questions, asked kindly. The view from above, for a night when something feels enormous. These are tiny hinges. A door swings on them anyway. Third, be specific. A vague sense that it helped won't hold up on a hard day. A real moment will: a time, a place, what you would have done, what you did instead. Marcus wrote book one that way. Not my teachers were good, but from this one person, this one thing. Fourth, the week behind us. We chose three habits to keep, and one idea to leave. We reread our notes from the first day of the porch. We thanked a freed slave, a flawed courtier, and an emperor who wrote to himself. Today we gather the proof, in our own lives, that any of it mattered. Tomorrow, just as honestly, the other side.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the year scroll back, slowly. Don't look for a big transformation. Look for one moment. A reply you held back. A worry you set down. A loss you met a little more steadily. A morning you began with a clear intention instead of your phone. When one comes, stay with it. Where were you? What would you have done before? What did you do? If it worked, there, once, let yourself notice it. If nothing comes, that's worth knowing too. The bell holds the time.
Where it worked: one real, specific moment when Stoic practice changed what you did, the wool and milk, not the grass. Today's word.
